messages.subject: Collinearity between simple predictors and their higher-order interactions
messages.subject_clean: Collinearity between simple predictors and their higher-order interactions
messages.body_plain:
Hello,



I've conducted a reading experiment with a 2 (Prime Type: DO prime vs. SC
prime) x 2 (Target Ambiguity: Ambiguous SC vs. Unambiguous SC) factorial
design. I am using a mixed-effect regression approach to investigate how
the effect of structural priming will change over time during the
experimental session. I regressed RTs onto the factorial design of Prime
Type, Target Ambiguity, and Presentation Order.  I also included
log-transformed character length as a control predictor to control for
length differences present in items.



The fixed effect structure:
cPrimeType*cTargetAmbiguity*cPresOrder+clogLength



First of all, "Prime Type" and "Target Ambiguity" were dummy-coded by using
"treatment" coding. Then, all of the fixed effects were centered before
submitted to the mixed-effect model to reduce collinearity. Log-likelihood
ratio tests were used to determine the maximal random effect structure for
the data set (Baayen, Davidson, & Bates, 2008; Jaeger, 2009).



The summary of the model contained a table of the correlations of the fixed
effects. The correlation table suggested collinearity between the simple
predictors and their higher-order interactions. For example, the
interaction between "Target Ambiguity" and "Target Ambiguity x Prime Type"
was .57. The interaction between "Presentation Order" and "Target Ambiguity
x Presentation Order" was .53. (The highest value of variance inflation
factor was 1.64.) In order to interpret estimated coefficients of each term
accurately, I need to deal with the collinearity present in the model.



I didn't know how to proceed with this collinearity problem. I have already
centered the fixed effects before the submission. Residualizing "Prime
Type" on "Target Ambiguity" (or vice versa) did not make sense to me since
both are manipulated categorical factors...  And including the higher-order
interactions is necessary to test my research hypotheses which were formed
prior to the experiment...



I am also puzzled by the fact that all of the correlations of the fixed
effects become under .09, when the model includes by-subject and by-item
random intercepts but not random slopes (whose inclusion has been justified
by model comparison).



Thank you very much for any comments on this matter in advance!!



Sincerely yours,



Sunfa Kim

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sunfa,

> (The highest value of variance inflation factor was 1.64.) In order to 
> interpret estimated coefficients of each term accurately, I need to 
> deal with the collinearity present in the model.
>

If the VIF is that low then I wouldn't worry. I always consider 4 to be 
the cut-off -- I've seen higher numbers suggested elsewhere, so I may be 
being conservative!

If you take the square root of the VIF then it'll tell you how much 
larger the standard error would be if the predictors were orthogonal. So 
if you divide the SE of the predictor with the highest VIF by 1.28 
(sqrt(1.64)) and it's still a reasonable distance from 0 then it should 
be fine.

HTH,

Ian

messages.subject: Re: Collinearity between simple predictors and their higher-order interactions
messages.subject_clean: Collinearity between simple predictors and their higher-order interactions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sunfa Kim,

what you're seeing is not unusual for *logistic* models. Even though you
have a balanced design it can occur that even after centering you still
have collinearity. But it seems you ran a linear model? For those cases,
I've seen similar behavior when there are ceiling or floor effects. But
given that you're seeing the correlations only when you include random
slopes I suspect that either (a) you don't have much data (e.g., do you
have more cases than 20* (# of fixed + # of random variances + # of random
covariances)?) and/or (b) your subjects actually differ quite a bit with
regard to how they are affected by the manipulations (and the correlations
emerge after that is taken into account). For example, it could be that
some of your subjects don't show any effects and the ones that do show
effects do not form a subsample in which your design factors are balanced
(a nice by-subject lattice plot will reveal that).

What to do? First, while work in my lab tries to keep fixed effect
correlations below .3 and VIFs below 2, that's primarily because we use
models with many covariates on unbalanced data and that makes me want to be
extra conservative. In relatively small balanced designs with a good number
of subjects, I think fixed effect correlations of .7 or higher result in
detectable loss of power (and, yes, as Ian says, VIFs <=4 are an often
cited cutoff; but note that the VIFs do not take into consideration that
correlations might only emerge after between-subject&item differences
--random intercepts and slopes-- are taken into consideration!). So, I
would worry about it, especially if model comparison confirms your results.
Keep in mind that collinearity only leads to biased standard error
estimates and *de*crease in power, i.e. *in*creased Type II error. So, if
you find significant effects, you're fine. The coefficient estimates
obtained from a model with collinearity are unbiased, although for highly
collineary effects, the coefficient estimate might be more unstable (depend
more on the specific sample you have). I haven't seen a systematic study of
this (might just be my ignorance) and, in any case, your fixed effect
correlations are acceptable.

HTH,

Florian

messages.subject: problem with pvals.fnc
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I'm a PhD student at the graduate school "Frequency effects in language" at the University of Freiburg in Germany. My PhD project is a longitudinal study in second language acquisition and I am currently trying to model my data in lmer - but now I've run into an lmer problem concerning pvals.fnc.

Stefan Gries suggested submitting the problem to this list.
The problem is the following:

My model (simplest version below) looks very similar to Harald Baayens lexdec3.lmerD3a (Baayen 2008: 255), but I can't run the pvals function:

> model.tokenskorrcloze  <- lmer(KorrP1ObligatorKontexte ~ InputTypfreq*Time + (1|Lerner.ID) + (0 + Time|Lerner.ID), data = tab)
> pvals <- pvals.fnc(model.tokenskorrcloze, withMCMC = T, nsim = 5000)
Fehler in pvals.fnc(model.tokenskorrcloze, withMCMC = T, nsim = 1000) : 
  MCMC sampling is not implemented in recent versions of lme4
  for models with random correlation parameters

For a brief model description:
dependent variable KorrP1ObligatorKontexte = number of correctly provided targets in compulsory contexts at test (numeric)
predictor variable InputTypfreq = treatment condition, four-level factor
predictor variable Time: three-level factor (pretest, mid-test, posttest)
random intercept: individual participants
random slope: individual development of participants over time (basically speed/amount of learning)

I used to work with R 2.10.1 and it didn't work, I've updated to 2.15.1 but it does still not work...

It seems that the relevant difference to Baayen's model is that in my case the random slope parameter, "Time", is a three-level factor (VT = pretest, ZwT = mid-test, NT = posttest, while in Baayen's model it's (0+Trial|Subject), i.e. numeric).
What seems to happen is that in this case lmer posits a correlation parameter for the random slope even for the 0+ case which in itself does not specify such a correlation parameter:

> model.tokenskorrcloze  <- lmer(KorrP1ObligatorKontexte ~ InputTypfreq*Time + (1|Lerner.ID) + (0 + Time|Lerner.ID), data = tab)
> model.tokenskorrcloze
Linear mixed model fit by REML 
Formula: KorrP1ObligatorKontexte ~ InputTypfreq * Time + (1 | Lerner.ID) +      (0 + Time | Lerner.ID) 
   Data: tab 
   AIC   BIC logLik deviance REMLdev
 761.2 808.2 -366.6    726.4   733.2
Random effects:
 Groups    Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr        
 Lerner.ID (Intercept) 1.28314  1.13276              
 Lerner.ID TimeVT      0.29944  0.54721              
           TimeZwT     0.84647  0.92004  0.235       
           TimeNT      3.87735  1.96910  0.550 0.628 
 Residual              0.22228  0.47147              
Number of obs: 212, groups: Lerner.ID, 72I

On Harald Baayen's suggestion I've tried to run the model without the random intercept, but this does not help, the correlation is still there:

> model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRI  <- lmer(KorrP1ObligatorKontexte ~ InputTypfreq*Time + (0+Time|Lerner.ID), data = tab)
> pvals <- pvals.fnc(model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRI, withMCMC = T, nsim = 5000)
  for models with random correlation parameters
Fehler in pvals.fnc(model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRI, withMCMC = T, nsim = 5000) : 
  MCMC sampling is not implemented in recent versions of lme4
  for models with random correlation parameters

I can only run pvals.fnc for the model without random slope:

> model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRS  <- lmer(KorrP1ObligatorKontexte ~ InputTypfreq*Time + (1|Lerner.ID), data = tab)
> pvals <- pvals.fnc(model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRS, withMCMC = T, nsim = 5000)
> pvals
$fixed
                         Estimate MCMCmean HPD95lower HPD95upper  pMCMC Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)                1.8000   1.8036     0.3642     3.2169 0.0164   0.0251

TimeZwT                    0.0000  -0.0116    -1.7650     1.9352 0.9952   1.0000
TimeNT                     0.6000   0.5870    -1.2967     2.4416 0.5356   0.4000
InputTypfreqhigh:TimeZwT   0.8419   0.8931    -1.1875     3.0402 0.4004   0.2976
InputTypfreqlow:TimeZwT    1.2972   1.3293    -0.5820     3.3754 0.1764   0.0891
InputTypfreqmid:TimeZwT    1.1842   1.2249    -0.6264     3.2940 0.2156   0.1218
InputTypfreqhigh:TimeNT    1.4526   1.4680    -0.5086     3.5916 0.1724   0.0705
InputTypfreqlow:TimeNT     2.3459   2.3588     0.2560     4.2486 0.0172   0.0022
InputTypfreqmid:TimeNT     2.0286   2.0339     0.0395     4.0276 0.0468   0.0081
$random
     Groups        Name Std.Dev. MCMCmedian MCMCmean HPD95lower HPD95upper
1 Lerner.ID (Intercept)   1.3883     0.7402   0.7404     0.5697     0.9263
2  Residual               1.1255     1.4807   1.4825     1.3251     1.6363
etc.

Unfortunately, omitting the random slope results in the loss of a substantial part of explanation of variance:

> (cor(fitted(model.tokenskorrcloze), TokensP1KorrClozeOhneNA))^2   # with random intercept + slope
[1] 0.9928922
> (cor(fitted(model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRI), TokensP1KorrClozeOhneNA))^2  # with random slope only
[1] 0.9769679
> (cor(fitted(model.tokenskorrcloze.withoutRS), TokensP1KorrClozeOhneNA))^2 # with random intercept only
[1] 0.80891

I do not use pvals.fnc for model comparison but I need it as a prerequisite for plotting my model data (mostly the interactions) using plotLMER (unless there was some other way of running plotLMER without prior application of pvals.fnc?).
As some of the t-values (basically for interactions _:TimeZwT) change substantially from the model comprising random intercept and slope to the model comprising the intercept only, the corresponding confidence intervals of plotLMER based on the model without random slope are way too conservative.

Thus:
Is there a way to tell R that I do not want it to add the correlation parameter in spite of "Time" being a factor, in order to be able to run pvals.fnc on the model comprising random intercept and 0+ slope without this mysterious correlation parameter?
Is there an older/a different version of lme4 that might be able to handle the problem?

Thank you very much for your help.
Karin.

messages.subject: Analysis of Categorical Outcomes: Away from mixed-effect models and back to ANOVAs?
messages.subject_clean: Analysis of Categorical Outcomes: Away from mixed-effect models and back to ANOVAs?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I guess most of the users of the list are aware of the submitted paper by Barr et al. on the use of maximal random effect structure for the evaluation of the significance of fixed effects in mixed-effect models. I personally find the paper convincing. But it leads to problems when confronted with real data and more complex designs, especially when you are dealing with categorical outcomes (lots of my work is on speech perception with a 2AFC task, so this standard for me).

In my experience, a model with more than 8 random slopes tends not to converge if you use the lmer function with a logistic linking function. And in speech-perception research that happens a lot, classically one presents a speech continuum in two condition, so a 2 x7 design is common (e.g., the classical Ganong-type experiments with a 7-step /s/ and /f/ continuum in  two contexts, gira.... (/f/ bias) and platypu... (/s/ bias)). A model such as the following:

lmer( f ~ continuum*bias + (continuum*bias|Subject), ...., family = binomial) 

is quite unlikely to converge. I asked around a bit, and I am not the only one experiencing this. If you would now even have an item effect as well, the chances of convergence are approaching zero quite quickly with models with a maximal random effect structure for subject and items.

In the rare case a model does converge, the fixed effects of the model lead to pretty bad predictions for the cell means. That is, usually I would like to see that the Intercept parameter of the model, if transformed back to proportions, matches the observed proportion in the cell of the design that is mapped on the Intercept. Similarly, I would like a good match between the observed proportions in the different cells of the design and the predicted proportions from the fixed effects. How does one interpret a model, that predicts quite different proportions for the different cells than the ones that are observed? 

After all, we really care about differences in the descriptive data, because usually theories predict differences between observed values in different conditions. The only reason to use inference statistics is that we need a yardstick to know what kind of difference in the descriptive data we should take seriously. So I am pretty bothered by the fact that the statistical model predicts quite different means than the ones I observe.

So does this mean: Back to ANOVAs with logistic or inverse-normal distribution transformation of individual cell means? This has been around for a while, under the name of Signal-detection theory, so it seems quite acceptable to me. Or how can we deal with failures to converge, which are quite common with categorical outcomes?

Kind regards,
Holger Mitterer


PS: A preemptive strike: If you want to propose the solution to treat continuum as a numerical variable, so that there would only be three random slopes to fit, read the following:

One obvious solution would be to treat continuum as a numerical variable, as this reduced the number of random slopes to be estimated. But this is problematic as well, because it severely constraints the possible form of the interaction. The bias is either constant (no interaction), gets larger at the /f/ end of the continuum (interaction < 0) or at the /s/ end (interaction > 0). But such a model would not be able to capture the (common) pattern that the effect of bias is maximal in the middle of the continuum.

If one does not want to specify beforehand what form of interaction is possible, one can either try all kinds of complicated stuff with polynomials (I'd rather not and doubt that such an option would be easily interpretable for the field) or use the continuum as a categorical predictor, so that the fitted model can accommodate how the binary variable (the lexical bias in this case) influences the perception of the sounds for each step individually.




- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 
Holger Mitterer, Ph.D.
Max-Planck-Institut für Psycholinguistik
Postbus 310
6500 AH Nijmegen
The Netherlands

messages.body_plain:
> I guess most of the users of the list are aware of the submitted paper by Barr et al. on the use of maximal random effect structure for the evaluation of the significance of fixed effects in mixed-effect models. I personally find the paper convincing. But it leads to problems when confronted with real data and more complex designs, especially when you are dealing with categorical outcomes (lots of my work is on speech perception with a 2AFC task, so this standard for me).
> 
> In my experience, a model with more than 8 random slopes tends not to converge if you use the lmer function with a logistic linking function. And in speech-perception research that happens a lot, classically one presents a speech continuum in two condition, so a 2 x7 design is common (e.g., the classical Ganong-type experiments with a 7-step /s/ and /f/ continuum in  two contexts, gira.... (/f/ bias) and platypu... (/s/ bias)). A model such as the following:
> 
> lmer( f ~ continuum*bias + (continuum*bias|Subject), ...., family = binomial) 
> 
> is quite unlikely to converge. I asked around a bit, and I am not the only one experiencing this. If you would now even have an item effect as well, the chances of convergence are approaching zero quite quickly with models with a maximal random effect structure for subject and items.

Moreno Coco and I are currently working on evaluting a model selection
function using Barr et al's simgen code, both on their artificial
dataset and a more complex artificial dataset. Our more complex
artificial dataset has one response generated by three fixed effects,
two fixed interactions, two random slopes, and three random intercepts.
All variables are continuous. Even when given the true generative
structure, the maximal random effects structure did not converge once
in 100,000 random datasets.

> After all, we really care about differences in the descriptive data, because usually theories predict differences between observed values in different conditions. The only reason to use inference statistics is that we need a yardstick to know what kind of difference in the descriptive data we should take seriously. So I am pretty bothered by the fact that the statistical model predicts quite different means than the ones I observe.
> 
> So does this mean: Back to ANOVAs with logistic or inverse-normal distribution transformation of individual cell means? This has been around for a while, under the name of Signal-detection theory, so it seems quite acceptable to me. Or how can we deal with failures to converge, which are quite common with categorical outcomes?

Perhaps it depends on your application. I like to look at corpus data,
and so it is important to control for correlations due to common talker
or common sentence. The model selection function we're evaluating is
located at http://jkpate.net/cocoSelect.R, and perhaps it would be
appropriate for your scenario. It does exhibit a few points of
anticonservativity relative to the maximal random effects structure on
the Barr et al datasets (obtaining a type I error rate of about 0.086
with a critical value of 0.05), but manages to converge on the more
complicated datasets.

It is, unfortunately, uncomfortably anti-conservative on the complicated
datasets, although the anticonservativity decreases as the number of
observations per level of each grouping factor increases. Specifically,
type I error rates at a critical value of 0.05 range from about 0.10 to
0.23, depending on dataset size, whether we allow correlated slopes,
and how significance is assessed. Specifically, forcing independent
slopes and using mcmc is most anticonservative, using the anova
function is least. This forward-selection method is much less
anticonservative than standard multiple regression, which obtains a
type I error rate of about 0.43. 

We're still examining exactly how sensitive the type I error rate is to
this aspect of the data (the resulting datasets become fairly large,
with several thousand observations, making monte carlo simulations
quite slow). 


-- 
John K Pate http://jkpate.net/
